messages.subject: pushed print statements
parts:
I pushed the change for print statements.

commit 016eec2c3a183fe3b56d98ef26cc3eb84ab35a45
Author: Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>
Date: Mon Sep 17 17:34:13 2012 -0400

added print statements to Stan language; still need doc and to push through RStan


In models, print statements are now allowed
anywhere statements are, with:

print(<expr>,...,<expr>);

where <expr> is any Stan expression.

The writes write the expression text then its value.

Prints in transformed data execute once as
data's read in. Prints in transformed params
and models execute once per leapfrog step.
Prints in generated quantities execute once
per iteration.

I followed the pattern we'd set up for
std::cerr and just threaded a pointer
to std::cout the same way, adding a
std::ostream* argument and setting a default to 0.
So hopefully it'll all be backward compatible
and RStan will still work as is.

RStan should then follow the command in
gm/command.hpp in setting the output stream.

I kept the streams separate so we could, in principle,
write domain errors to std::cerr and print statements
to std::cout. As is, the command sets both streams
to std::cout. Printing can be turned off by not
setting them or using the unset methods in the
base mcmc/adaptive_sampler class.

I could modify print so that we can print arbitrary
user strings, too. If we do that, I won't print the
expression text automatically. The only test we need
on strings is that they're legal C++ strings (meaning
no unescaped double quotes).

The control from the top won't change if
the print statements change to allow strings and
every existing print statement would still work, which
is why I decided to push now.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] pushed print statements
parts:
On 9/18/12 11:35 AM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> So now we only allow print to print scalar variable?

Thanks for pointing out this issue. It hadn't
even occurred to me because I had C's printf() in
mind.

The way I implemented print with operator<<
should print matrices and scalars, but not arbitrary
arrays. I'll add an overload for std::vector<T> to
print recursively.

Which brings up the issue of how multivariate
variables should be rendered. Any suggestions?

Eigen implements << for its matrices, and it prints
them with newlines like matrices. I could change
this behavior by using something other than operator<<.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: multivariate variables
parts:
On Tuesday, September 18, 2012 2:10:54 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Which brings up the issue of how multivariate
variables should be rendered.  Any suggestions?

Eigen implements << for its matrices, and it prints
them with newlines like matrices.  I could change
this behavior by using something other than operator<<.

I kind of like Eigen's printed output, but don't have a strong opinion about that. So, I'll just threadjack to another issue with multivariate variables.

Suppose you have a parameterized covariance matrix and 1000 draws from the posterior distribution. The "average covariance matrix", which puts the posterior mean of each covariance into a matrix, may not be positive definite. Same with the median and so on. In a manner of speaking, that is the "right" answer. But it might be useful in some circumstances to first average over the primitive parameters and then transform that to get a covariance matrix that is positive definite. Except the primitive parameters don't get written. Maybe it would be useful for RStan to have R functions that transformed back to the primitive parameters?

Ben

On Tue, Sep 18, 2012 at 3:12 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Tuesday, September 18, 2012 2:10:54 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:

>>

>> them with newlines like matrices. I could change
>> this behavior by using something other than operator<<.
>>
>
> I kind of like Eigen's printed output, but don't have a strong opinion about
> that. So, I'll just threadjack to another issue with multivariate variables.
>
> Suppose you have a parameterized covariance matrix and 1000 draws from the
> posterior distribution. The "average covariance matrix", which puts the
> posterior mean of each covariance into a matrix, may not be positive
> definite. Same with the median and so on. In a manner of speaking, that is
> the "right" answer. But it might be useful in some circumstances to first
> average over the primitive parameters and then transform that to get a
> covariance matrix that is positive definite. Except the primitive parameters
> don't get written. Maybe it would be useful for RStan to have R functions
> that transformed back to the primitive parameters?

Actually, the mean matrix will be positive definite. Quick proof: if
x'Ax > 0 and x'Bx > 0 for all x !=0, then x'(A+B)x = x'Ax+x'Bx >0 for
all x != 0. The median though, as you point out, may not be.

The functions your suggesting may be useful, but I feel like they may
be beyond the scope of Stan/RStan in that users of these functions
should understand what those transformed variables are in order to use
them properly. It may turn out at some future point that Stan no
longer uses the same transform (or maybe not even transformed
parameters at all) at which point these functions don't make much
sense or will break user expectations.

To put it another way:

1) Functions which expose the internal coordinates used by Stan are
probably a bad idea in my view.
2) Functions which transform between unconstrained and constrained
representations of variables like covariance matrices are a good idea
but is more generic than Stan.

Cheers,
Marcus

parts:
On 9/18/12 3:12 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Tuesday, September 18, 2012 2:10:54 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> Which brings up the issue of how multivariate
> variables should be rendered. Any suggestions?
>
> Eigen implements << for its matrices, and it prints
> them with newlines like matrices. I could change
> this behavior by using something other than operator<<.
>
>
> I kind of like Eigen's printed output, but don't have a strong opinion about that. So, I'll just threadjack to another
> issue with multivariate variables.

So do I, but I like the idea of putting it all in one line, too.
I don't like basic print operations that span multiple lines.
Probably too much line-based processing historically.

It does bring up the question of where to start and how
to deal with new lines.
If someone writes

print("x=",x);

and x is a 2x2 matrix, would we print

x=[[1,2],
[3,4]]

>
> Suppose you have a parameterized covariance matrix and 1000 draws from the posterior distribution. The "average
> covariance matrix", which puts the posterior mean of each covariance into a matrix, may not be positive definite.

I was wondering about how likely this would be in practice,
but Marcus's neat proof convinced me :-) I should've
remembered that from the matrix book -- addition and positive
scaling are both positive definiteness preserving.
> Same with the median and so on.

Simplexes are OK! So are ordered variables.

I see the problem with medians, which brings up the
issue of whether we want computations for medians in
Stan -- there's nothing in there to compute them
(at least that I recall -- I'm working on the function
indexing).
> In a manner of speaking, that is the "right" answer.

This whole non-linear transform business is fraught with peril.

Like the sqrt of the unbiased estimator for variance
not being an unbiased estimator for sd.

And var(X) having different convergence properties
than X.

> But it might be useful in some
> circumstances to first average over the primitive parameters and then transform that to get a covariance matrix that is
> positive definite.

I can imagine the answer would be different because
of the non-linearity in the transforms.

We're usually measuring convergence on the constrained
variables, though Andrew had said earlier he'd rather
do it on the unconstrained ones because the normality
assumptions are more reasonable there (and maybe for
other reasons I forget).

> Except the primitive parameters don't get written. Maybe it would be useful for RStan to have R
> functions that transformed back to the primitive parameters?

I think that's a good idea for other reasons, too.

But I think Marcus has a good point about not wanting to tie
them too closely to the underlying bits of Stan.

All the transforms are available in stan/prob/transform.hpp
by the way, so the coding wouldn't be too hard.

- Bob
